title: Jacobian Aligned Random Forests
one_liner: Use one global supervised rotation before training a forest, so simple axis-aligned splits can follow feature interactions that would otherwise require many awkward tree cuts.
lead: Ordinary decision trees split one feature at a time. That is fast and stable, but it becomes wasteful when the real decision boundary depends on a combination of features rather than on any single coordinate. In those cases, an axis-aligned tree needs many small rectangular partitions to approximate one slanted or interaction-driven boundary. Oblique trees address this by learning a fresh linear combination at many nodes, but that adds optimization cost and extra instability. This paper asks whether one carefully chosen global transformation is enough. JARF first fits a standard forest, then estimates how the output changes when each input feature is perturbed. From those change directions it builds one shared rotation and scaling map. A second forest trained in that transformed space can now use ordinary one-feature thresholds more directly because the important joint directions have already been lined up with the coordinate axes.

problem.h2: Why axis-aligned trees waste splits on rotated structure
paras: A tree threshold on one feature works well when the target changes mostly along that one coordinate. It works poorly when the target changes along a slanted direction such as a weighted sum of several features.

In that slanted setting, the tree must stack many single-feature splits to approximate one important boundary. That increases depth and can fragment the data into many small leaves. Oblique trees fix the coordinate mismatch by learning a different hyperplane at each node, but the added optimization makes them slower and more complex. The paper looks for a middle ground: keep simple trees, but rotate the input space once using supervision from the target.

callout.html: Estimate which input directions change the prediction most, then rotate the whole feature space once so plain threshold splits align with those directions.

steps.text: Train a standard random forest first, because it provides supervised predictions from which directional sensitivity can be estimated.

steps.b: Perturb each feature and measure output change.
steps.text: Use finite differences, which means small input nudges, to estimate how much the prediction changes along each coordinate.
Form an expected Jacobian outer product, meaning an average square table built from prediction-change directions, because this summarizes which combined feature directions matter globally.
Rotate and rescale the input space using that square table, because the strongest supervised directions should become easier for axis-aligned splits to isolate.

steps.b: Train a second forest in transformed coordinates.
steps.text: Reuse ordinary axis-aligned splits in the new space, because the hard interaction structure was handled by the preprocessing step.

paras: The paper changes where oblique structure is handled. Instead of learning a new slanted split at every node, it learns one global supervised preconditioner before building the final forest.
object.object: where the model pays the cost of handling feature interactions

hidden.name: the global table of important prediction-change directions
paras: The decisive object is the average outer product of prediction-change directions. Each local change direction says how the output would move if one input moved slightly. Averaging their outer products builds a square table that highlights directions in feature space where supervised change is consistently strong.

That square table matters because it captures interactions without learning a separate split formula at each node. If a diagonal direction repeatedly changes the prediction, the transformation can turn that diagonal into a coordinate axis. After that, a one-feature threshold is no longer a poor approximation of the true boundary.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the shared supervised coordinate map extracted before the final forest is trained.

reads.html: The method tries to discover which directions in the input space really move the prediction, then it turns those directions into the axes the tree will split on.

JARF uses an expected Jacobian outer product, meaning an average square table built from prediction-change directions, to define a single global preconditioner that aligns feature interactions with axis-aligned tree splits.

mechanism.h2: Why one global rotation can be enough
paras: A forest does not need the original coordinates specifically. It only needs coordinates in which simple thresholds separate useful regions. If most of the supervised signal lies along a few combined directions, then a global transformation can expose those directions before any tree is built.

The first forest supplies the directional information. By checking how predictions move under small coordinate perturbations, JARF estimates which combinations of features the target is most sensitive to. Averaging those local sensitivities stabilizes the estimate, because one noisy sample does not control the whole transformation.

The second forest benefits because the transformed coordinates already encode interaction structure. That means a shallow axis-aligned split can represent what would have required several layered thresholds before. Training stays simpler than in oblique forests because the trees themselves still optimize only one-feature cuts.

math.words: Average the outer product of the prediction-change direction at many points. Large directions in that average matrix mark combined feature directions that repeatedly affect the output.
math.equation: shared_geometry = mean over data points of outer_product(prediction_change_direction, prediction_change_direction)
symbols: the finite-difference estimate of how the model output changes when inputs are nudged
a matrix that records which coordinate combinations move together in that direction
the average across many samples so the geometry is global rather than tied to one example
the matrix used to rotate and rescale features before the final forest

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the target changes most when feature 1 rises while feature 2 also rises.
At many data points, the prediction-change direction therefore points roughly along the same combined direction.
Averaging the outer products keeps that shared direction prominent and suppresses isolated noisy directions.
The transformation then rotates that shared direction toward one axis.
After rotation, a tree can separate the classes with a short threshold chain instead of many rectangular patches.

math.note: The forest remains axis-aligned after transformation; the oblique behavior is moved into the preprocessing step.

charts.title: Plain axis-aligned forest on rotated structure
charts.note: It trains quickly, but it spends too many splits approximating boundaries that are not aligned with the raw coordinates.

charts.title: JARF with shared supervised rotation
charts.note: The transformed coordinates let simple thresholds follow the important combined directions, so the forest keeps much of the speed advantage of ordinary trees.

items.b: One global transformation cannot match every local pattern.
items.html: If different regions of the data need very different boundary orientations, a single shared rotation may still leave some regions misaligned because the best direction varies across the space.

items.b: The first forest can estimate the wrong directions.
items.html: If the baseline forest is too weak or too noisy, the prediction-change directions will be unreliable, which means the transformation can emphasize the wrong feature combinations.

items.b: Finite-difference estimates can be unstable on rough outputs.
items.html: When small perturbations cause irregular prediction changes, the sensitivity estimate becomes noisy, so the shared direction table may need enough averaging to remain useful.
When the data share a clear global orientation, JARF works well because one supervised rotation removes much of the coordinate burden from the final forest.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create tabular classification tasks where the boundary depends on a slanted combination of two or three features. Compare an ordinary random forest, an oblique-forest baseline, and JARF.

The demo should report accuracy, average tree depth, and training time. A convincing result shows JARF approaching the oblique baseline with less training cost because the global rotation turns the important interaction directions into coordinates that ordinary splits can use directly.
demo.metric_eq: split_burden = mean over trees of internal_split_count
demo.closing: The paper's claim is specific: a single supervised change of coordinates can recover much of the benefit of oblique splits when the interaction pattern is broadly shared.
